event_topic: Science Olympiad Division B Disease Detectives
prompt: A single-meal retrospective cohort of 120 enumerated attendees had two correlated food exposures X and Y. Joint-group counts after the meal: both X and Y: 50 attendees, 30 cases; X only: 10 attendees, 6 cases; Y only: 10 attendees, 1 case; neither: 50 attendees, 5 cases. All attendees were followed. Using the supplied definitions (confounding vs effect modification) and the two analysts’ approaches (Analyst 1: marginal/crude RRs; Analyst 2: conditional/stratified RRs from the four joint groups), state which analyst’s report should guide selection between foods for operational prioritization and give that prioritized food (non-causal wording). Show computations for marginal and conditional attack rates and RRs and your interpretation.
solution_steps: Compute marginal attack rates and crude RRs for X and Y from marginals.
Compute conditional (stratified) attack rates and RRs using the four joint groups for Y within X strata and for X within Y strata.
Compare marginal and conditional RRs to see whether marginal associations persist after conditioning.
Use supplied definitions: if marginal association disappears on conditioning, call it confounding; if conditional RRs differ across strata, call it effect modification.
Decide which analyst to follow and give an operational (non-causal) priority.
solution:
Step 1 — Marginal (crude) RRs.
- For X: exposed = both + X only = 50+10 = 60 attendees; cases = 30+6 = 36; AR_exposed = 36/60 = 0.6. Unexposed = Y only + neither = 10+50 = 60; cases = 1+5 = 6; AR_unexposed = 6/60 = 0.1. Crude RR_X = 0.6 / 0.1 = 6.0.
- For Y: exposed = both + Y only = 50+10 = 60; cases = 30+1 = 31; AR_exposed = 31/60. Unexposed = X only + neither = 10+50 = 60; cases = 6+5 = 11; AR_unexposed = 11/60. Crude RR_Y = (31/60) / (11/60) = 31/11 ≈ 2.8182.

Step 2 — Conditional (stratified) RRs from joint groups.
- Y within X=present: Y present (both) AR = 30/50 = 0.6; Y absent (X only) AR = 6/10 = 0.6; RR_Y|X=present = 0.6/0.6 = 1.0.
- Y within X=absent: Y present (Y only) AR = 1/10 = 0.1; Y absent (neither) AR = 5/50 = 0.1; RR_Y|X=absent = 0.1/0.1 = 1.0.
- X within Y=present: X present (both) AR = 30/50 = 0.6; X absent (Y only) AR = 1/10 = 0.1; RR_X|Y=present = 0.6/0.1 = 6.0.
- X within Y=absent: X present (X only) AR = 6/10 = 0.6; X absent (neither) AR = 5/50 = 0.1; RR_X|Y=absent = 0.6/0.1 = 6.0.

Step 3 — Compare and interpret.
- Marginal: RR_X = 6.0; RR_Y ≈ 2.8182. Conditional: RR_Y is 1.0 in both X strata (effect disappears when conditioning on X). RR_X is 6.0 in both Y strata (effect persists unchanged when conditioning).
- By the supplied definitions, Y’s marginal association is explained by confounding with correlated X (marginal association disappears on conditioning). Conditional RRs do not differ across strata, so there is no effect modification.

Step 4 — Recommendation.
- Analyst 2 (stratified analysis) should guide operational prioritization. Operational (non-causal) priority: investigate/prioritize food X.
rubric: 1 point: Correct marginal attack rate and RR for X (AR_exposed=36/60=0.6, AR_unexposed=6/60=0.1, RR_X=6.0).
1 point: Correct marginal attack rate and RR for Y (AR_exposed=31/60, AR_unexposed=11/60, RR_Y=31/11 ≈ 2.8182).
1 point: Correct conditional RRs for Y within X strata (RR_Y|X=present = 1.0; RR_Y|X=absent = 1.0).
1 point: Correct conditional RRs for X within Y strata (RR_X|Y=present = 6.0; RR_X|Y=absent = 6.0).
1 point: Correct classification: Y’s marginal association is due to confounding by X; no effect modification (conditional RRs equal across strata).
1 point: Correct operational conclusion: follow Analyst 2 and prioritize food X (stated as an operational priority, not causal proof).

solution_first_blueprint.target_skill: interpret stratified retrospective cohort data to prioritize exposures
solution_first_blueprint.novel_context: A single-meal retrospective cohort of 120 enumerated attendees with two correlated food exposures (X and Y) served together to varying subsets.
fixed_givens: Total attendees = 120, all enumerated and followed identically
Joint exposure groups after the meal: both X and Y: 50 attendees, 30 cases; X only: 10 attendees, 6 cases; Y only: 10 attendees, 1 case; neither: 50 attendees, 5 cases
Attack rates and risk ratios (RRs) are appropriate (cohort, complete follow-up)
Analyst 1 reports marginal (crude) RRs for each food separately
Analyst 2 reports conditional (stratified) RRs computed from the four joint groups

Supplied definitions to use: confounding = a non-causal mixing of effects where marginal association is distorted by a correlated factor; effect modification = true variation in effect size of an exposure across levels of another variable
assumptions: No misclassification of exposure or outcome
No loss to follow-up or selection bias
No other exposures or covariates affect the comparisons
All arithmetic must match the provided exact numeric results
solution_steps: Compute marginal (crude) attack rates and RRs for X and Y from the 2x2 marginal tables: group counts sum to totals; compute exposed and unexposed case proportions and RRs.
Compute conditional (stratified) attack rates and RRs using the four joint groups: for Y within X=present and X=absent; for X within Y=present and Y=absent.
Compare marginal and conditional RRs to assess whether the marginal association for a food persists when conditioning on the other food.

Apply the supplied definitions to decide whether observed patterns indicate confounding (marginal change that disappears on conditioning) or effect modification (different conditional RRs across strata).
State which analyst's complete report should guide selection between foods and give an operational (non-causal) priority.
solution_first_blueprint.expected_answer: Analyst 2. Marginal (crude) RRs: X crude RR = 6.0; Y crude RR = 31/11 ≈ 2.8182. Conditional (stratified) RRs from the four joint groups: conditional Y RRs within X=present and X=absent = 1.0 and 1.0; conditional X RRs within Y=present and Y=absent = 6.0 and 6.0. Interpretation using supplied definitions: Y’s marginal association is explained by confounding with correlated X (marginal RR for Y disappears when conditioned on X); there is no effect modification (conditional RRs are equal across strata). Operational recommendation (bounded, non-causal): prioritize investigating food X as the target for traceback/control, explicitly noting this is an operational priority, not proof of causation.
solution_first_blueprint.uniqueness_check: All numbers and comparisons are fully determined by the given four-group counts; marginal and conditional RRs compute uniquely to the stated exact values, so the conclusion (Analyst 2; prioritize X without claiming causation) is uniquely determined by the data and supplied definitions.
distractor_mechanisms: Pick-the-higher-marginal-RR: choose Y solely because crude RR for Y (≈2.82) seems notable without checking stratified data.
Confuse confounding with effect modification: claim equal conditional RRs indicate effect modification rather than confounding.
Ignore joint-group data: report only Analyst 1’s marginal RRs and recommend Y while dismissing stratified contradictions.

non_obvious_decisions: Prefer stratified conditional RRs over marginal RRs when joint-group data are available and contradict crude associations

Use the supplied definitions to label the pattern as confounding (marginal association disappears on conditioning) rather than effect modification (would require differing conditional RRs across strata)
Formulate an operational (non-causal) priority rather than asserting causation

mechanisms.name: Marginal-only comparison (Analyst 1)
core_chain: Compute crude (marginal) attack rates and RRs for X and Y using the two-by-two marginal tables.
Compare crude RRs: larger RR gets priority for initial suspicion.
Report the marginal RRs and recommend focusing on the food with the higher crude RR.
indispensable_decisions: Treat marginal (population-level) RRs as the decisive summary for selecting a suspected exposure versus treating joint-group (stratified) comparisons as decisive.
Assume no hidden correlation between exposures that would distort marginal comparisons unless additional evidence is requested.
mechanisms.shortcut_to_rule_out: Ignore the four joint-group data (X&Y, X-only, Y-only, neither) and avoid stratified RRs.

mechanisms.name: Stratified joint-group comparison (Analyst 2 — defensible)
core_chain: Use the four enumerated joint exposure groups (both, X only, Y only, neither) to compute conditional attack rates and RRs.
Compute conditional RRs for Y within levels of X and for X within levels of Y.
Compare marginal and conditional RRs to determine whether marginal associations are stable or change when conditioning on the other exposure.
Base selection on the stratified/conditional comparisons when they contradict marginal results, and present both sets of RRs in the report.
indispensable_decisions: Treat stratified (conditional) RRs computed from the four joint groups as decisive when they differ from marginal RRs, rather than relying solely on marginal RRs.
Interpret pattern of equal conditional RRs across strata as evidence that one exposure's marginal association is due to confounding by the other exposure (not effect modification).
mechanisms.shortcut_to_rule_out: Rely only on marginal RRs or only on single-exposure summaries without using the joint-group stratified comparisons.

mechanisms.name: Causal-diagram/backdoor reasoning with the four-group evidence
core_chain: Propose two plausible causal representations: (A) X is an actual cause and X and Y are correlated because Y is contingent on the same meal (Y is non-causal confounder), or (B) Y is an actual cause and X is correlated non-causally, or (C) X and Y interact (effect modification).
Use the observed marginal and conditional RRs from the four-group table to test which causal representation is inconsistent with the data.

Rule out representations whose predicted conditional/marginal patterns conflict with observed RRs; select the representation consistent with the observed equal conditional RRs for Y and persistent X effect.
Report the chosen causal representation as a non-causal-priority (operational recommendation) while explicitly acknowledging lack of proven causation.
indispensable_decisions: Choose between alternative causal-graph hypotheses (X causal, Y causal, or interaction) as the formal representation to be tested by the data, rather than treating the data as a neutral summary only.
Accept or reject a causal representation on the basis of whether its implied pattern of marginal versus conditional RRs matches the observed joint-group RRs.
mechanisms.shortcut_to_rule_out: Treat the problem merely as arithmetic comparison without positing and testing alternative causal representations that make distinct observable predictions.

difficulty_architecture.selection_reason: Mechanism 2 (stratified joint-group comparison) directly uses the fully enumerated four joint groups to compute the conditional RRs that resolve the apparent marginal association for Y; it contains the required non-obvious decision to prefer stratified over crude summaries and the subsequent rule-out of confounding versus effect modification, matching the exact given results and instruction to prioritize X without claiming causation.
mandatory_solution_structure: State crude (marginal) attack rates and RRs for X and Y (crude X RR = 6.0, crude Y RR = 31/11 ≈ 2.82).

Show conditional (stratified) RRs computed from the four joint groups: conditional Y RRs (within X=present and X=absent) = 1.0 and 1.0; conditional X RRs (within Y=present and Y=absent) = 6.0 and 6.0.
Answer which complete report should guide selection between the foods (Analyst 2) and justify using the conditional RRs.
Using the supplied explicit definitions, state whether the pattern indicates confounding or effect modification and why (Y is confounded by correlated X; no effect modification).
Give a bounded non-causal operational recommendation: prioritize investigating X (operational priority) but do not assert causation.
closure_requirements: All arithmetic and attack-rate/RR values must match the provided exact results.
Provide both marginal and conditional RRs exactly as specified.
Explicitly reference the supplied definitions when distinguishing confounding from effect modification.
Conclude with the prioritized target (X) and a statement that this is an operational priority, not a causal proof.
forbidden_shortcuts: Deciding by applying a supplied formula or threshold without comparing alternative representations (e.g., 'pick the higher RR' alone).
Selecting a named formula or model as decisive without showing it rules out other plausible representations.
Using unit conversion, rote arithmetic, or restating definitions as the non-obvious decisions required by the task.
Relying on a single-template 'pick the highest marginal RR' approach that ignores joint-group stratified evidence.

event_topic: Science Olympiad Division B Disease Detectives
prompt:
Three-site surveillance across two periods. Use only longitudinally comparable subsets (per assumptions): Site A both periods; Site C only old-definition counts (exclude C’s 60 new-only cases); exclude Site B from before–after network inference (no Period 1). Reference standard population for direct standardization: 50% young, 50% older. Data:
- Site A Period 1: young pop=2,000 with 20 cases; older pop=8,000 with 320 cases (same definition both periods).
- Site A Period 2: young pop=8,000 with 120 cases; older pop=2,000 with 100 cases (same definition both periods).
- Site B Period 1: absent; Site B Period 2: pop=5,000 with 50 old-definition cases.
- Site C Period 1: pop=5,000 with 25 old-definition cases.
- Site C Period 2: pop=5,000 with 30 old-definition cases plus 60 new-only cases (incomparable, exclude for trend).
Tasks: Using only comparable subsets, report (numbers as proportions×100): A) A crude rates Period1→Period2 and A age-specific rates; B) A direct-standardized rates (50/50 standard) Period1→Period2; C) C harmonized old-definition rates Period1→Period2; D) State whether a network-wide decline is supported and give one recommended next surveillance action.
answer: A crude 3.4% → 2.2%; A young 1.0% → 1.5%; A older 4.0% → 5.0%; A age-standardized 2.5% → 3.25% (50/50 standard); C harmonized old-definition 0.5% → 0.6% (exclude C’s 60 new-only); Reject network-wide decline; A and C (harmonized) increase. Recommend: adopt common case definitions and require age-stratified reporting and baseline participation (get Site B Period 1).
solution_steps: Exclude Site B from before–after network inference because Period 1 baseline is missing.
Compute Site A age-specific and crude rates for each period, then apply direct standardization (50% young, 50% older).
Compute Site C harmonized old-definition subset rates (exclude 60 new-only cases for trend).
Compare crude vs. age-specific vs. standardized results and interpret whether the network-wide decline claim is supported.
State a single recommended next surveillance action to improve future network comparisons.
solution:
Step 1: Exclude Site B from before–after inference (no Period 1). Exclude C’s 60 new-only cases for longitudinal comparison.
Site A Period 1:
- young rate = 20 / 2,000 = 0.010 = 1.0%
- older rate = 320 / 8,000 = 0.040 = 4.0%
- crude = (20+320) / (2,000+8,000) = 340 / 10,000 = 0.034 = 3.4%
Site A Period 2:
- young rate = 120 / 8,000 = 0.015 = 1.5%
- older rate = 100 / 2,000 = 0.050 = 5.0%
- crude = (120+100) / (8,000+2,000) = 220 / 10,000 = 0.022 = 2.2%
Note: Both age-specific rates in A rose (young 1.0%→1.5%; older 4.0%→5.0%) while crude fell (3.4%→2.2%), suggesting an age-composition artifact.
Direct standardization for A with 50% young/50% older standard:
- Period 1 standardized = 0.5*(1.0%)+0.5*(4.0%) = 2.5%
- Period 2 standardized = 0.5*(1.5%)+0.5*(5.0%) = 3.25%
Site C harmonized old-definition (exclude 60 new-only cases):
- Period 1 = 25 / 5,000 = 0.005 = 0.5%
- Period 2 = 30 / 5,000 = 0.006 = 0.6%
Interpretation: Age-specific and standardized rates for A increase (2.5%→3.25% standardized); C harmonized old-definition rate increases (0.5%→0.6%). Therefore the director’s claim of a network-wide decline is not supported when using longitudinally comparable data. Do not include B or C’s new-only cases in before–after inference.
Recommended next surveillance action: require common case definitions and age-stratified reporting and ensure baseline participation (obtain Site B Period 1) so future network comparisons are valid.
rubric: 1 point: Correct A period-1 crude rate = 3.4% (340/10,000).
1 point: Correct A period-2 crude rate = 2.2% (220/10,000).
1 point: Correct A age-specific rates: young 1.0%→1.5%; older 4.0%→5.0%.
1 point: Correct A direct-standardized rates (50/50 standard): 2.5%→3.25%.
1 point: Correct C harmonized old-definition rates: 0.5%→0.6% (excluded 60 new-only cases).

1 point: Correct interpretation and recommendation: reject network-wide decline; conclude A and C (harmonized) trends rise; recommend common definitions, age-stratified reporting, and baseline participation (Site B Period 1).

solution_first_blueprint.target_skill: surveillance time-trend interpretation with age adjustment
solution_first_blueprint.novel_context: Three-site, two-period surveillance with one site changing age composition and one site broadening case definition
fixed_givens: Site A Period 1: young pop=2,000 with 20 cases; older pop=8,000 with 320 cases (same definition both periods)
Site A Period 2: young pop=8,000 with 120 cases; older pop=2,000 with 100 cases (same definition both periods)
Site B Period 1: no data (absent); Site B Period 2: population=5,000 with 50 old-definition cases
Site C Period 1: population=5,000 with 25 old-definition cases
Site C Period 2: population=5,000 with 30 old-definition cases PLUS 60 new-only cases after broadening the definition (60 must be treated as incomparable for longitudinal comparison)
Reference standard population for direct standardization: 50% young, 50% older
assumptions: Use only longitudinally comparable subsets: full A both periods, C only old-definition counts (exclude C's 60 new-only cases for trend), exclude B from before–after network inference because it lacks Period 1
Age groups for A are 'young' and 'older' as given; C has only old-definition aggregate counts (no age breakdown) so age-specific standardization applies only where age strata are available (A)
solution_steps: Exclude Site B from network before–after inference because Period 1 baseline is missing.
Compute Site A age-specific and crude rates for each period:
Note both age-specific rates in A rose from Period 1 → Period 2 (young 1.0% → 1.5%; older 4.0% → 5.0%).
Compute Site C harmonized-old-definition subset rates (exclude 60 new-only cases for trend):
C Period 1 old-definition rate = 25 / 5,000 = 0.005 = 0.5%.
C Period 2 old-definition rate = 30 / 5,000 = 0.006 = 0.6%.
Apply direct standardization to Site A using the supplied 50% young / 50% older standard:
A standardized Period 1 = 0.5*(young rate 1.0%) + 0.5*(older rate 4.0%) = 0.5*(0.01 + 0.04) = 0.025 = 2.5%.

Interpretation: A's crude rate fell (3.4% → 2.2%) while age-specific rates and the age-standardized rate rose (2.5% → 3.25%), indicating the crude decline is an age-composition artifact. C's harmonized old-definition rate rises (0.5% → 0.6%) when comparing comparable subsets. B cannot be used for before–after inference.

Conclusion: The director's claim that incidence declined network-wide is rejected. The strongest supported temporal conclusion is that longitudinally comparable site-specific trends (Site A and Site C using the harmonized old-definition subset) both increase. Do not extrapolate to Site B or compute a pooled adjusted network rate.

Single recommended next surveillance action: require common case definitions and age-stratified reporting plus ensure baseline participation (i.e., make B report Period 1) so future network comparisons are valid.

Accept A’s crude decline at face value as evidence of falling risk—misleads by ignoring the age-composition reversal and age-specific rates.
Include Site B in before–after adjusted comparisons by imputing or assuming a Period 1 baseline—misleads by inventing absent data instead of excluding B.

Exclude C’s 60 new-only cases from longitudinal comparison and retain only C’s harmonized old-definition subset.

event topic: Science Olympiad Division B Disease Detectives
prompt: Investigators enrolled 40 cases (30 ate Food X, 10 did not). Two available control samples each contain 80 noncases: community-registry controls (ate X = 20, did not = 60) and clinic controls (ate X = 50, did not = 30). Community controls were sampled independently of exposure from the source population that produced the cases. Clinic controls were selected because they sought care for an unrelated condition that is associated with eating Food X. No population denominators or sampling fractions are known. Analyst 1 proposes: “Use the clinic controls and report the sampled case exposure proportion divided by the sampled clinic-control exposure proportion as a population risk ratio.” Explain why Analyst 1’s proposal is invalid, name the defensible control choice, choose the appropriate measure of association for these data, and give the numeric results for (a) the defensible analysis using the chosen controls, (b) the clinic-control analysis for sensitivity, and (c) Analyst 1’s reported sampled proportion ratio. Provide only the concise answer (no justification).
answer: Use community-registry controls and report an odds ratio. Community OR = 9.0; clinic OR = 1.8; Analyst 1 sampled-proportion ratio = 1.2; 1.2 is NOT a valid population RR and the true RR is not identifiable (clinic controls biased).
solution_steps: Choose the control group that best represents the exposure distribution in the source population (community-registry controls, since clinic selection is associated with exposure).
Decide which measure is identifiable given fixed case and control totals and unknown population denominators: use the odds ratio rather than treating sampled exposure proportions as population risks.
Compute community OR: (30×60)/(10×20) = 9.0.
Compute clinic OR (sensitivity): (30×30)/(10×50) = 1.8.
Compute Analyst 1’s reported sampled-proportion ratio: (30/40)/(50/80) = 0.75/0.625 = 1.2.
Conclude Analyst 1’s 1.2 is not a population RR here (population risks not identifiable) and clinic-control selection related to exposure biased the clinic-based estimate toward the null.
solution: Analyst 1’s proposal is invalid because clinic controls were selected in a way related to exposure and because case-control sampling fixed totals so sampled exposure proportions do not equal population risks when population denominators/sampling fractions are unknown. The defensible control group is the community-registry controls (sampled independently of exposure). The identifiable measure is the odds ratio. Using community controls: OR = (30×60)/(10×20) = 9.0. Using clinic controls (sensitivity): OR = (30×30)/(10×50) = 1.8. Analyst 1’s reported sampled-proportion ratio = (30/40)/(50/80) = 1.2, which is not a valid population risk ratio here; the true population RR is not identifiable and the clinic-based estimate is biased toward the null.
rubric: 1 point: explicitly choose community-registry controls as the defensible control group.
1 point: explicitly state the appropriate measure is the odds ratio (not a sampled RR).
1 point: compute and give community OR = 9.0 and clinic OR = 1.8.
1 point: compute Analyst 1’s sampled-proportion ratio = 1.2 and state it is not a valid population RR and that the true RR is not identifiable (clinic control selection biased).

solution_first_blueprint.novel_context: A single outbreak with 40 enrolled cases and two available control samples (community registry and clinic patients); evaluate an analyst's proposal that treats clinic-control exposure proportion as a population risk and propose the defensible alternative analysis.
fixed_givens: Total cases enrolled = 40
Cases who ate Food X = 30
Cases who did not eat Food X = 10
Two control groups available, each with 80 noncases
Community-registry controls: ate X = 20, did not = 60 (n=80)
Clinic controls: ate X = 50, did not = 30 (n=80)
No population denominators or sampling fractions are known
Analyst 1 proposal (given): use clinic controls and compute sampled case exposure proportion divided by sampled control exposure proportion and report that as a risk ratio
assumptions: All 40 cases and all 80 controls in each control sample are the observed sample counts; case and control totals are fixed by the sampling design
Community-registry controls were sampled independently of exposure from the source population that produced the cases
Clinic controls were selected because they sought care for an unrelated condition that is associated with eating Food X (selection related to exposure)
No further population incidence or sampling-fraction information is available, so population risks (true RRs) are not directly identifiable
solution_steps: Decide which control group better represents the exposure distribution in the source population that produced the cases. Because clinic selection is linked to eating X, choose community-registry controls as the defensible control group.

Decide which measure of association is identifiable given case-control sampling that fixes case and control totals. prompt:
A school has 100 students. A one-day fair occurred on Day5. A cafeteria item was served Days3–8. Common-source incubation = 2–5 whole days; secondary onset after close contact = 3–5 whole days. First-wave onsets (total 28): Day7=4, Day8=14, Day9=8, Day10=2, Day11=0. Among those 28: fair attendees who became cases = 24 of 40; fair nonattendees = 4 of 60. Among those 28: cafeteria consumers = 15 of 50; cafeteria nonconsumers = 13 of 50. Of 72 non-first-wave students: 20 had documented close contact with a symptomatic first-wave case on Day9 and 10 of these became ill later; among the 52 without such contact, 1 became ill later. Later onsets: Day12=2, Day13=7, Day14=2, then zero. No other shared exposure is known. Day arithmetic is exact. State Models 1, 2, and 3 below and submit a compact evidence memo that selects one model and rejects the others based on the provided data.

Model 1: Single point-source exposure on Day5 (fair) producing the first-wave cases, with limited secondary spread.
Model 2: Continuous common-source exposure from the cafeteria served Days3–8 producing first-wave cases (no meaningful secondary spread).
Model 3: Independent second point-source exposure (not Day5) producing the later onsets; first-wave cause uncertain. Identify the best model and give the decisive evidence (do not list every intermediate arithmetic step).
answer: Model 1: Day5 point source (fair) followed by limited secondary spread. Evidence: intersected exposure date = Day5; fair RR = 9.0 (24/40 vs 4/60); cafeteria RR ≈1.15 (15/50 vs 13/50) is weak; contact RR = 26.0 (10/20 vs 1/52) and Day9→Day12–14 onsets match 3–5 day secondary interval.
solution_steps: Reverse-incubation for each first-wave onset: Day7→exposure Day2–5; Day8→Day3–6; Day9→Day4–7; Day10→Day5–8. Intersection = Day5.
Compute first-wave attack rates and RRs: fair attendees 24/40=60.0% vs nonattendees 4/60=6.67% → RR = 9.0. Cafeteria consumers 15/50=30.0% vs nonconsumers 13/50=26.0% → RR ≈1.15.
Compute later-case risks by Day9 contact: contacted 10/20=50.0% vs not-contacted 1/52≈1.92% → RR ≈26.0.
Verify timing: documented close contact on Day9 → later onsets Day12–14 = 3–5 days, consistent with secondary transmission interval.

Synthesize: unique exposure-date intersection (Day5) and very large fair RR implicate Model 1; weak cafeteria RR and timing contradict Model 2; strong, time-consistent contact-stratified RR argues against Model 3 as an independent second point source.

2) Calculate attack rates among first-wave: fair attendees 24/40 = 60.0%; fair nonattendees 4/60 = 6.67%; RR = 60.0 / 6.67 = 9.0, a very strong association. Cafeteria consumers 15/50 = 30.0%; nonconsumers 13/50 = 26.0%; RR = 30.0 / 26.0 ≈ 1.15, a weak association inconsistent with a dominant continuous Days3–8 source.
3) Later onsets: among 72 others, those with documented Day9 close contact had 10/20 = 50.0% illness vs 1/52 ≈ 1.92% for others; RR ≈ 26.0. The contacts occurred on Day9 and later onsets were Day12–14 (3–5 days later), matching the known secondary generation interval.

Model 2 is rejected because the cafeteria RR ≈ 1.15 is too weak and its multi-day exposure window contradicts the unique Day5 intersection. Stratify dessert by chicken: among chicken eaters, dessert risk 18/30 = 60% vs non-dessert 6/10 = 60%, RR = 1.0. Among non-chicken eaters, dessert risk 2/10 = 20% vs non-dessert 0/10 = 0%, RD = 20 percentage points (RR undefined). 3) Chicken shows the more consistent association (persists in both dessert strata). 4) Biological model: favor preformed-toxin given vomiting and 1–3 h onset. Non-chicken eaters = dessert only (10) + neither (10) = 20; ill = 2+0 = 2 → risk = 2/20 = 10%. RR_chicken = 60% / 10% = 6.0. 2) Stratify chicken by dessert status. Among dessert eaters (both vs dessert-only): chicken+dessert = 30 with 18 ill → 18/30 = 60%; dessert-only = 10 with 2 ill → 2/10 = 20%; RR = 60%/20% = 3.0. core_chain: Present raw 2x2 cross-tab (no derived values)
Student must compute crude risks and risk ratios for each food
Student must stratify by the other food (dessert ↔ chicken) and compute within-stratum risks and RRs or RDs
Compare whether association for each food persists in both strata
Decide which food remains most consistently associated and prioritize actions accordingly
indispensable_decisions: How to interpret persistence vs heterogeneity of association across strata (i.e., treat stable elevated RR in both strata as stronger evidence vs treat sparse/heterogeneous stratum as ruling the food out)
How to balance crude vs stratified evidence when associations conflict (choose the exposure whose association is consistent bidirectionally)
mechanisms.shortcut_to_rule_out: Ruling out the dessert solely because one stratum is sparse or shows weaker crude RR (must consider within-stratum persistence for chicken)

mechanisms.name: Toxin-vs-infectious-timing plausibility plus stratified data
core_chain: Present symptoms/time-to-onset and the same cross-tab
Student must use vomiting-predominant 1–3 hour onset to favor a preformed toxin hypothesis over an enteric infection (non-obvious model choice)
Then compute crude and stratified measures to see which food best fits toxin pattern and data consistency
Decide which food to prioritize for control given both epidemiologic and biological-plausibility evidence
indispensable_decisions: Choose between preformed-toxin model and infectious-agent model based on incubation and symptoms
Weigh biological-plausibility model against stratified epidemiologic persistence when selecting a single food to restrict
mechanisms.shortcut_to_rule_out: Selecting the causal mechanism solely from crude RRs without considering incubation/profile (must make and justify toxin vs infectious decision)

mechanisms.name: Handler-cross-contamination vs intrinsic contamination inference with stratification
core_chain: Give cross-tab plus statement 'no known symptomatic handler' and access to roster/records
Student must decide whether cross-contamination from an asymptomatic handler or intrinsic contamination of one food is more plausible
Compute crude and stratified measures to see which food’s association persists across strata to infer intrinsic contamination vs cross-contamination
Choose control/follow-up prioritizing either product removal/traceback or focused handler investigation accordingly
indispensable_decisions: Decide between asymmetric cross-contamination hypothesis (single contaminated food contaminates the other at serving) and intrinsic contamination hypothesis (one food itself contaminated independently)
Decide whether absence of symptomatic handler sufficiently downgrades handler-mediated hypotheses given epidemiology and records
mechanisms.shortcut_to_rule_out: Assuming a symptomatic handler is required to accept handler-mediated cross-contamination (asymptomatic carriers or improper handling can still cause contamination)

difficulty_architecture.selection_reason: Mechanism 1 directly forces the required bidirectional stratified evidence decisions and yields the exact contrast set the prompt specifies; it contains two non-obvious representational choices and leads to a compact, closed student target.
mandatory_solution_structure: Report crude risks and RRs for chicken and dessert (no derived values in prompt)
Report within-dessert stratum contrasts for chicken: 18/30 vs 2/10, RR=3
Report within-non-dessert stratum contrasts for chicken: 6/10 vs 0/10, RD=60 percentage points and RR undefined
Report within-chicken stratum contrasts for dessert: 18/30 vs 6/10, RR=1
Report within-non-chicken stratum contrasts for dessert: 2/10 vs 0/10, RD=20 percentage points and RR undefined
Report crude chicken contrast: 24/40 vs 2/20, chicken risk 60% vs 10%, RR=6.0
Report crude dessert contrast: 20/40 vs 6/20, dessert risk 50% vs 30%, RR≈1.67
Describe dessert evidence as heterogeneous and sparse (does not fully disappear)
Make two explicit non-trivial decisions (which representation/model to trust; whether persistence across both strata is decisive)

Produce an authority-bounded control/evidence/follow-up package that at minimum: stops access to implicated food without discarding/redistributing it, preserves evidence/records with chain-of-custody, notifies/defers to public health authority, and prioritizes lab confirmation, handler history/interviews, and trace-back
closure_requirements: Solution must not claim causation—only association and prioritization
All listed contrasts and numerical results above must be present exactly
Control plan must explicitly state stopping access (no redistribution/discard) and preserving items for testing with chain-of-custody
Must include notifying and deferring to public-health statutory authority as a top-priority action
Must prioritize laboratory confirmation, handler history/interviews, and product trace-back in that order of evidence follow-up
forbidden_shortcuts: Do not place the decisive interpretation rule (e.g., 'if association persists in both strata, choose that food') into the student prompt
Do not rely on recall of named formulas or applying supplied thresholds as the non-obvious decision
Do not treat simple arithmetic or unit conversion as one of the required non-obvious decisions
Do not present derived contrasts or RRs in the student-facing prompt (only raw cell counts allowed)
